segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, a podcast that takes Dickens's great, sprawling, infuriating masterpiece and opens it up — chapter by chapter, image by image.
I'm your host, and today we begin at the very beginning — the novel's famous opening, where Dickens greets us not with a character or a plot, but with weather.
Fog, to be precise.
I'm joined today by three people who know this novel inside out and bring very different kinds of attention to it.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who thinks harder about how Dickens builds his sentences than almost anyone alive.
When Eleanor reads a passage, she sees the architecture behind the prose — and she makes you see it too.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian with a speciality in Victorian institutions — Chancery, the Poor Law, the whole machinery of a society that could be utterly indifferent to suffering.
He brings the real world crashing into the fiction, and the collision is always illuminating.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it five times since.
She cares deeply about the experience of reading — what moves you, what makes you laugh, what makes you stop and read a line again.
Let's begin with the fog.
The extraordinary thing about this opening is that Dickens doesn't begin with a person, or a house, or even an event.
He begins with a condition — a condition that, as we come to understand, is the novel's true subject.
The fog is everywhere, and so is the system of law that the fog comes to represent.
Listen to how Dickens establishes that ubiquity.

"Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city."
That word "defiled" is doing enormous work.
It isn't a meteorological term — it's a moral one.
From the very first paragraph, Dickens is telling us that the fog is not merely atmospheric — it is ethical.
And notice what he does structurally with that fog — the anaphora, that relentless repetition of the word at the start of each clause.
"Fog up the river... fog down the river... fog on the Essex marshes... fog on the Kentish heights."
It performs the very thing it describes — the fog accumulates, clause by clause, until you feel you can't breathe.
This is Dickens using syntax as weather.
And then he scales it down — from the sweeping geography of the river to something devastatingly specific.
"Fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of his shivering little 'prentice boy on deck."
That single child — unnamed, cold, pinched by fog that is described as acting with intent — contains the whole novel's moral argument in miniature.
What strikes me, every time I read that opening, is the pity in it.
Dickens is describing a world, yes — but he is also grieving it.
The "ancient Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards" — there's such tenderness in that detail.
These are people entirely forgotten by the system, tucked away in their wards, with the fog finding them even there.
And I agree with James entirely — that word "defiled" lodges in you.
Dickens had a preacher's instinct for the word that carries weight beyond its dictionary meaning.
And then — as if he has established the fog as a general catastrophe — Dickens marches us directly to its source.
The fog is thickest, he tells us, at a very specific address.

"The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction, appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old corporation, Temple Bar."
Now, Temple Bar is not merely a landmark — it was the gateway between the City of London and the legal quarter, the literal threshold of the law.
Dickens knew this perfectly well, and his readers knew it too.
"Leaden-headed" does triple duty — it means heavy, it means dull, and it means lead-coloured, the grey of fog and of a system that has lost its light.
That superlative construction — "rawest," "densest," "muddiest" — is another piece of virtuoso Dickens craft.
He doesn't just say the fog is thick near Temple Bar — he says it is at its most extreme there.
The law is the apex of the fog, the place where obscurity achieves its purest form.
And then Dickens delivers the sentence that, for me, is one of the great rhetorical set-pieces in English prose.

"This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance."
That catalogue — madhouse, churchyard, ruined suitor — moves from the abstract to the grotesquely specific, and it never lets you look away.
That sentence is the one I come back to, every single time.
Because it's not describing Chancery in the abstract — it's describing what Chancery has done, everywhere, to everyone.
The "worn-out lunatic in every madhouse" — Dickens isn't being melodramatic.
There were real people driven to breakdown by decades of Chancery litigation.
And the ending — "Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here" — that's not rhetoric, that's a verdict.
The system condemns itself, out of the mouths of its own practitioners.
Caroline is entirely right to press on the literal truth of that.
The Court of Chancery, at the time Dickens was writing, was in genuine crisis — cases that had lasted forty, fifty, sixty years were not unknown.
The system was not corrupt in the sense of bribery — it was corrupt in a more insidious way: it was structurally incapable of resolving the disputes it was meant to adjudicate.
So when Dickens writes about "walls of words" and "mountains of costly nonsense," he is not inventing — he is reporting.
And that phrase — "walls of words" — is so good it almost hurts.
Language, which for Dickens is the supreme instrument of humanity and feeling, has been turned by Chancery into a weapon of obstruction.
The fog and the words are the same thing — both impenetrable, both choking, both serving the interests of those who profit from confusion.
There is one more image I want us to sit with before we move on — Chesney Wold in autumn, which comes later in the novel but belongs spiritually to this same fog-world.
Dickens describes the great house shut up for the season, the ancestors retreating from the light.
And then comes this extraordinary phrase, which I read slowly every time.
"The dead and buried Dedlocks walk there in the long nights and leave the flavour of their graves behind them."
"The flavour of their graves" — I don't know how he arrived at that word, "flavour," but it is the precisely wrong word that becomes precisely right.
Graves don't have flavour — but somehow you know exactly what it smells and tastes like, that cold, blank, churchyard air.
Fog, mud, walls of words, and the flavour of graves — Dickens has set his stage with extraordinary care.
Everything that follows will be played out against this backdrop of systemic, atmospheric, almost supernatural obscurity.
After the break, we'll meet the people who have to live inside that fog — beginning with the suitors themselves and the strange world of Esther Summerson.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart — slowly, carefully, and with considerable affection.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most heartbreaking arcs: the unraveling of Richard Carstone.
Charming, talented, fundamentally decent — and destroyed, inch by inch, by Chancery.
With me today are three people who know this novel deeply and bring very different lenses to it.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with total absorption in how it works.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who can tell us exactly what Chancery was, what it did to people, and why Dickens was right to be furious about it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has never quite recovered — which is, I think, exactly the right response.
Let's begin at the beginning of Richard's story — not the end, though we'll get there — with Esther's early diagnosis of what's wrong.
Eleanor, Esther sees it before anyone else does, doesn't she?
She does, and what's remarkable is that Esther never sounds censorious about it.
She genuinely likes Richard — she's at pains to tell us so — and yet she can see the fault line running straight through him.
What Dickens does here that I find structurally brilliant is to locate the problem not in Richard's character alone, but in the system that formed him.
The passage is worth reading closely, because the sentence Dickens builds is itself an enactment of what he's describing.
"They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters."
The pivot on 'but' is everything — good qualities, yes, but directed by what?
That reversal — servant becoming master — is the entire architecture of Richard's tragedy compressed into one antithesis.
And Dickens doesn't leave it there: 'If they had been under Richard's direction, they would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction, they became his enemies.'
He doubles the construction — chiasmus, almost — to make sure you feel the inversion, not just understand it.
And it matters enormously that Dickens pins this on education — on the system — rather than simply on Richard's weakness of will.
Victorian readers would have recognized that critique immediately.
The great public schools of the period operated on exactly the uniformity Dickens describes — the same curriculum, the same floggings, the same Latin verses, regardless of aptitude or temperament.
Richard isn't a failure — he's a product.
And the novel then delivers him into a second system — Chancery — which is equally indifferent to individual capacity, and which will finish what school began.
What strikes me every time I re-read this passage is Esther's tone.
She's fond of him.
She lists his qualities — 'quick abilities, good spirits, good temper, gaiety and freshness' — and you feel she means every word.
Which makes the 'but' that follows all the more devastating, because it arrives with sorrow rather than judgment.
Esther isn't condemning Richard.
She's mourning what he might have been.
And we're only in the early chapters — the tragedy is just beginning to announce itself.
That mourning is precise and structural, too — Dickens has set up the dual narration so that Esther's retrospective voice always knows more than the moment she's describing.
When she writes 'I felt more and more,' that repetition isn't accident — it's accumulation.
She's watching something worsen across time, and the syntax enacts the watching.
And then — and this is where Dickens does something I genuinely love — he switches narrators entirely for the middle chapters of Richard's decline.
The omniscient narrator takes over, and suddenly we're standing outside Richard rather than watching him through Esther's sympathetic eyes.
The effect is chilling — and the passage in Chapter 39, the Lincoln's Inn passage, is one of the finest things in the book.
Dickens writes — and I want to read this in full, because the rhythm is doing so much work here:

"On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour."
That list — bent head, bitten nail, lowering eye, lingering step — it's a portrait built from fragments, each detail a small ruin.
And then 'the good consuming and consumed' — the chiasmus again, the devouring made reciprocal — that phrase alone is worth the price of the novel.
That passage has enormous historical resonance, because Lincoln's Inn and the Inns of Court were genuinely littered with these figures.
Chancery suitors who had been waiting years, sometimes decades, for a resolution that would never come.
The real Jarndyce v Jarndyce — the cases Dickens was drawing on — some of them ran for forty, fifty years.
Dickens is absolutely precise when he writes 'Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent.'
"Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is very rich in such precedents; and why should one be different from ten thousand?"
That final question — 'why should one be different from ten thousand?' — is the cruelest possible deployment of institutional logic.
The system doesn't care that this particular lounger is young, gifted, and salvageable.
It has processed ten thousand before him, and it will process ten thousand more.
And what follows immediately in that chapter is even harder to read, because Dickens names exactly what the suit has done to Richard's mind.
He can no longer fight the abstraction — the suit is too vast, too shapeless to be an enemy.
So he does what damaged people do — he finds someone concrete to blame.
The line that undoes me every time is this one:
"injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat."
Shadows into substances — you can't win against something you can't see, so you manufacture a visible enemy.
And poor Jarndyce — who has only ever tried to protect him — becomes that enemy.
It's psychologically exact, and it's devastating.
It's exact in another way too — Richard's own words, later on, confirm the diagnosis with a kind of terrible lucidity.

There's a moment in Chapter 51 when he speaks to Woodcourt with complete candor — and it's one of the few times in the novel where a character sees himself clearly and it makes things worse, not better.
He says to Woodcourt:
"I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else."
And then — this is the moment that breaks my heart as a writer — he says:
"It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not."
'I think not' — he could have escaped, he half knows it, and he refuses the escape because to admit it would be to unmake himself entirely.
And then: 'Take me as I am, and make the best of me.' Which is the saddest possible thing to say to someone who loves you.
'The net into which my destiny has worked me' — that phrase does a great deal of legal and moral work simultaneously.
In Chancery, there was a genuine sense in which suitors were trapped: once you entered the suit, it was almost impossible to exit without resolution.
Your money, your energy, eventually your identity became entangled in the proceedings.
What's remarkable about Richard is that he entered the suit voluntarily — he chose the net — and yet that choice was itself conditioned by everything that came before.
His education, his expectations, his absence of other anchors — Dickens makes the case that the net was always there, waiting.
That physical decline in Chapter 60 is almost unbearable to read, precisely because we remember how vivid he was.
Esther catalogues it so carefully: 'thin and languid, slovenly in his dress, abstracted in his manner.'
Each adjective is another piece of Richard gone.
But the sentence that I always have to stop at — that I can never read past without pausing — is this:
"There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away."
A ruin of youth which is not like age.
Age is natural.
This is something else — a man hollowed out before his time, by forces entirely outside the scale of any normal human life.
And the most painful page is Chapter 51 — the passage on his false hopefulness — which I think is Dickens at the absolute summit of his psychological writing.
Esther draws a distinction that most novelists would never think to make:

"His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable."
'So conscious of being forced' — he knows the hope is performed, and he cannot stop performing it.
That is the specific texture of a particular kind of suffering that has barely been named before Dickens names it here.
And then the final blow — 'if the fatal cause could have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in that same hour' — even total victory would not have saved him.
The damage was already written in his face, indelibly, past any remedy the suit could offer.
That's the true horror, isn't it — not that Richard loses the case, but that winning it could never have returned him to himself.
Chancery doesn't merely consume money and time.
It consumes the self.
We'll return after a short break to look at what Dickens places around Richard — the parasitic figure of Vholes, and what he represents.
Stay with us.

segments.title: A Secret in the Shadows: Lady Dedlock and Narrative Concealment

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
I'm joined today by three readers who know this novel as well as anyone alive — and who disagree with each other in the most productive ways.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who can dissect a Dickens sentence the way a surgeon dissects — with genuine reverence for what she finds inside.

Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian whose knowledge of Victorian institutions — Chancery, the courts, the whole machinery of power — keeps us honest about what Dickens was actually describing.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt has read Bleak House five times and still finds new things to love and mourn in it — she's our close reader, our guide to the experience on the page.
Today we're looking at Lady Dedlock — one of the great secret-keepers in English fiction — and at the narrative machinery Dickens builds around her concealment.
Caroline, you've been wanting to start with that Lincolnshire opening for some time now.
I have, yes — because I think it's one of the most quietly devastating openings in the novel, and it's not always given its due.
Dickens doesn't introduce Lady Dedlock by describing her face or her manner — he introduces her through weather.
The whole Lincolnshire landscape is wrung out and waterlogged before she ever appears in it.
Listen to this passage — it's almost hallucinatory in its insistence:
"The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink."
Lead-coloured. Indian ink. Those are the colours of a woman who has buried something — pigments of suppression.
And then comes the tiny domestic scene — the child, the fire, the woman running out to meet a man at the gate — and Lady Dedlock is put quite out of temper by it.
She says she's been bored to death. But we know immediately she's been pierced to the heart.
What you're describing is Dickens using the pathetic fallacy — the landscape as emotional projection — but doing something cleverer than the usual Romantic version.
He never tells us Lady Dedlock is suffering. The landscape suffers instead, so that we feel her interiority without being let inside it.
That's the structural genius of it — the omniscient narrator sees everything and tells us almost nothing about what matters most.
And that drip, drip, drip on the Ghost's Walk — Dickens actually writes it out rhythmically, onomatopoeically — it's doing the work of a heartbeat, or a countdown.
The prose is already telling us this woman is haunted before we've been told what haunts her.
I want to add a layer to that — because the social machinery around Lady Dedlock is just as suffocating as the weather.
She is introduced through the fashionable intelligence — the press, essentially — as a commodity of spectacle, not a person.
Her movements are reported to the Parisians for their comfort — which is a brilliant little satirical cut — her entire life is constructed for the consumption of others.
So when she sees that keeper's lodge — that utterly ordinary scene of domestic warmth — the contrast is crushing.
She is childless, in a world where a woman's social value was inseparable from maternity — and Dickens marks that parenthetically, almost as if he doesn't want to draw attention to the wound.
But of course the parenthesis is the wound. The whole scene turns on it.
That parenthesis — 'who is childless' — is one of the great throwaway lines in Victorian fiction.
James is absolutely right — Dickens buries it mid-sentence and it detonates quietly.
Which brings me to what happens when we meet her again later in the novel alongside Tulkinghorn — because by that point the temperature has changed entirely.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary passage where the two of them are circling each other in plain sight, at dinner, for days on end.
"They meet again at dinner—again, next day—again, for many days in succession."
That repetition — again, again, again — is relentless. It has the rhythm of dread.
The repetition is doing everything there — it mimics the inescapability of the situation.
But what I find even more remarkable is how Dickens frames each of them — and the framing is character revelation disguised as social observation.
He sets this up with absolute precision:
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
Exhausted deity. Presiding at her own shrine. She is a goddess who despises her own cult — and we're meant to feel both the grandeur and the horror of that.
And then Tulkinghorn — 'the same speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home' — he's described as an object, a container.
She is a deity. He is a vault. And between these two monumental things, a secret is locked.
The vault metaphor is apt in ways Dickens may not entirely have intended — because Tulkinghorn is genuinely analogous to the Chancery system he operates within.
Chancery was precisely a repository — documents, deeds, wills, the accumulated secrets of families held in perpetuity and released to no one in useful time.
Tulkinghorn holds Lady Dedlock's secret the way the court holds the Jarndyce estate — as leverage, as power, at no benefit to anyone but himself.
And Dickens captures this standoff — the mutual suspicion, the perpetual alertness — with a sentence that I think is one of his finest rhetorical constructions.

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
'Hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.' That qualification — for the time — is the whole mechanism of the plot compressed into four words.
And then there's the scene in Chapter Forty — which I find almost unbearable to read, in the best possible sense.
Tulkinghorn is telling his Roman allegory — his coded accusation — and Lady Dedlock is sitting across from him in the firelight.
And Dickens gives us this:
"By the light of the fire he can be seen looking towards the moonlight. By the moonlight, Lady Dedlock can be seen in profile, perfectly still."
Perfectly still. Two words. The whole woman is in those two words.
Every instinct she has is to flee, or to weep, or to confess — and she does none of those things.
She performs stillness as armour. And the moonlight renders her in profile — like a medallion, like something already minted and fixed.
The chiastic structure of that sentence is worth pausing on — 'by the light of the fire he... by the moonlight, she' — it's a mirror construction.
Each illuminated by a different light source. Each visible to the other in a different register.
Firelight is warm, flickering, associated with the domestic and the human — that's his light. Moonlight is cold, remote, eternal — that's hers.
Dickens is encoding her tragedy into the grammar of the sentence without once stating it directly.
And then there's the moment — just a phrase, really — where the mask slips, just fractionally.
Tulkinghorn has been speaking of a supposed acquaintance who died — and Lady Dedlock wonders if he might be dead.
She means Tulkinghorn himself. And Dickens renders her thought — just barely — like this:
"a shade is on my Lady's face, as if she thought, 'I would he were!'"
A shade. Not a flush, not a flinch. A shade.
And notice how the narrator hedges even that — 'as if she thought.' Not 'she thought.' The certainty is withheld even from us.
Which is, I think, the most frightening thing in the passage — that even in her murderous wishing, she is not fully legible.
She is never fully legible. That's the whole tragedy and the whole achievement.
Dickens gives her dignity by withholding total access — we never quite possess her, and so she retains a kind of sovereignty even in her ruin.
Sovereignty in ruin — that might be the most exact phrase for Lady Dedlock I've ever heard.
We've been talking about the architecture of concealment — the landscape, the social performance, the lit faces in the dark.
In our next segment, we'll follow the secret as it begins to move — outward from Lady Dedlock, toward the characters who will be destroyed by it.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Blighted Street: Jo and Social Indifference

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens' great novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see what makes it so enduring — and so uncomfortable.
Today we're descending into Tom-all-Alone's — the ruined street at the heart of the novel's social argument — and into the life of Jo, the crossing-sweeper.
With me, as ever, are three remarkable readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose attention to how Dickens builds his effects — sentence by sentence — is frankly unmatched.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows what Chancery was, what Victorian poverty actually looked like, and why Dickens' anger is historically precise.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it with her whole heart — including a deep tenderness for its most overlooked characters.
James, let's begin with the place itself — Tom-all-Alone's — because Dickens' description of it is almost shockingly direct.
Tom-all-Alone's is one of the most precise slum portraits in Victorian fiction — and I use 'precise' deliberately, because Dickens had visited places very much like it.
The detail about bold vagrants seizing decayed houses and subletting them in lodgings — that was exactly the tenure pattern in rookeries like St. Giles or Jacob's Island.
But Dickens doesn't let description remain documentary.
He reaches for something that reads almost like a contagion map when he says — and the phrasing here is extraordinary —

"comes and goes, fetching and carrying fever and sowing more evil in its every footprint than Lord Coodle, and Sir Thomas Doodle, and the Duke of Foodle, and all the fine gentlemen in office, down to Zoodle, shall set right in five hundred years."
The Doodle passage is played for comedy — and it is funny — but what it does structurally is devastating.
It names the political class as explicitly insufficient — not corrupt, not evil, simply insufficient — while the slum's fevers do more damage than they could ever repair.
Five hundred years is not hyperbole by much, if you look at how slowly institutional reform actually moved.
That list of names — Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, Zoodle — is one of Dickens' great comic inventions, but you're absolutely right that the comedy is a kind of trap.
You laugh, and then the sentence closes with 'five hundred years,' and the laughter curdles.
What I find extraordinary is the simile he's working with before that — the vermin and the ruined tenements.
'As on the ruined human wretch vermin parasites appear, so these ruined shelters have bred a crowd of foul existence' — the architecture of that sentence is deliberately parallel.
The humans are mapped onto the buildings and vice versa, so you can't separate the social condition from the physical one.
And that coiling, crawling syntax — 'coils itself to sleep, in maggot numbers, where the rain drips in' — you feel it in your body as you read.
Dickens is making the prose physically uncomfortable so that we cannot remain detached observers.
What gets me, re-reading this passage, is that first sentence — 'Jo lives — that is to say, Jo has not yet died.'
That parenthetical correction is so quietly brutal.
Dickens doesn't say Jo is dying — he simply redefines what it means for Jo to live, and that redefinition happens in a subordinate clause, almost casually.
And then there's the image of Jo at Blackfriars Bridge — the cross of St. Paul's glittering above the smoke — which I find almost unbearably poignant.
Dickens sets it up so carefully:
"From the boy's face one might suppose that sacred emblem to be, in his eyes, the crowning confusion of the great, confused city — so golden, so high up, so far out of his reach."
So golden, so high up, so far out of his reach — that triple repetition lands like three quiet blows.
The cross is supposed to be a symbol of salvation, and for Jo it is simply one more beautiful, incomprehensible thing the city withholds from him.
And then, of course, he's told to move on — even there, even at that moment of stillness.
James, I want to turn to the great polemic in Chapter 16 — the passage where Dickens inhabits Jo's consciousness directly.
This is the passage that, for my money, has no equal in the novel for sheer controlled fury.
Dickens shifts from third person to a kind of intimate first — 'It must be a strange state to be like Jo!' — and suddenly the narrator is trying on Jo's experience.
It's a rhetorical device — the sustained conditional — but what it does is force the comfortable reader to imaginatively inhabit an existence they have never once considered.
And then he arrives at the heart of it:
"It must be a strange state, not merely to be told that I am scarcely human, but to feel it of my own knowledge all my life!"
'To feel it of my own knowledge' — that is the sentence that should stop every reader cold.
Because being told you are less than human can be resisted — but when the structures of society have been so thorough that you have internalised that verdict yourself, there is no appeal left.
That is not a Victorian problem.
The repetition of 'It must be' at the top and bottom of that passage is doing enormous work — it's the hinge the whole thing turns on.
The first 'It must be a strange state to be like Jo' is almost an invitation — come, imagine this.
By the time you reach the second — 'It must be a strange state, not merely to be told that I am scarcely human' — the grammar has shifted to 'I,' and the imagination is no longer optional.
Dickens has walked you into the trap so gradually you don't feel the walls close.
And then there's the parenthesis — 'as in the case of my offering myself for a witness' — which is anchoring the rhetoric in the legal reality.
Jo was literally rejected as a witness in the inquest on Nemo's death because he could not swear an oath he did not understand.
Dickens is reminding us that this is not metaphor — the dehumanisation has a legal document behind it.
There's something about the rhythmic accumulation of that passage that I find almost impossible to read aloud without feeling winded.
Dickens keeps adding weight — 'hustled, and jostled, and moved on' — and you feel Jo's exhaustion building inside the syntax itself.
And then: 'everybody overlooked me until I became the creature that I am.'
That word 'creature' — Dickens lets Jo use it of himself — is almost unbearable.
Because 'creature' is what you call something that is not quite a person, and Jo has absorbed that judgment so completely it has become his own vocabulary for himself.
James put his finger on exactly the right thing — the internalisation is what breaks you.
Jo's suffering doesn't stay contained within him — it spreads, and in a devastatingly literal way.
James, the passages about illness and contagion — Jarndyce on the hospital paradox, the accusation laid at Jo's door — what do those reveal about the novel's social argument?
The hospital passage is one I return to when I want to show students exactly what Dickens was doing with legal irony.
Jarndyce is pacing and rumpling his hair — Esther catches his physical agitation — and then he says:

"Is it not a horrible reflection, that if this wretched creature were a convicted prisoner, his hospital would be wide open to him, and he would be as well taken care of as any sick boy in the kingdom?"
The English Poor Law in 1852 did precisely this — a felon in gaol had more guaranteed medical access than a vagrant on the street.
Jarndyce's outrage is not rhetorical flourish — it is historically accurate, and Dickens knew it was accurate.
The system that punishes you offers you more protection than the system that merely ignores you.
That is a critique of institutional indifference that has not dated by a single day.
And then the woman's speech — the passionate accusation in Chapter 46 — which is formally quite strange, because Jo is being blamed for something done to him.
She says — and she's weeping as she says it, Dickens is careful to tell us she's breaking into passionate tears —
"the young lady that was such a pretty dear caught his illness, lost her beautiful looks, and wouldn't hardly be known for the same young lady now."
The woman genuinely loves Esther, genuinely grieves for her — but the logic of her accusation is the logic of the entire society: the poor carry contamination.
Jo didn't choose his illness, just as he didn't choose Tom-all-Alone's, but in both cases he is the vector — not the victim.
The cruelty of that reversal, and the fact that it comes from a woman who is not villainous but simply caught in the same prejudice — that's Dickens at his most devastating.
What I'd add is that the contagion plot is one of the novel's great structural achievements — and not just metaphorically.
Dickens is writing in the immediate aftermath of the 1848 cholera epidemic, when the miasma theory of disease was giving way — slowly and painfully — to germ theory.

He grasped, with a novelist's instinct rather than a scientist's proof, that poverty and disease move through society the same way: invisibly, across class boundaries, via the people the respectable world would rather not look at.
Jo infects Esther; Esther's disfigurement travels upward through the social register.
The plot is enacting the argument: you cannot wall off Tom-all-Alone's and remain untouched.
This is not sentimentality — it is a systems argument dressed in narrative form.
Exactly — and the ending of the Chapter 16 description is worth sitting with, because it closes on the most irreversible fact imaginable.
After everything — the strangeness, the exclusion, the verdict of barely-human — Dickens writes:
"His whole material and immaterial life is wonderfully strange; his death, the strangest thing of all."
We know from the novel's opening how it ends for Jo — and so does Dickens, writing this.
That sentence functions as a quietly placed epitaph, positioned in the middle of the novel, for a boy who has not yet died.
It is one of the coldest, most controlled acts of narrative foreshadowing I know of in English fiction.
That phrase — 'Jo has not yet died' — opened this passage, and now 'his death, the strangest thing of all' closes it.
Dickens wraps Jo's entire life in that grammatical bracket, and inside it is everything we've been discussing: the exclusion, the invisibility, the internalised verdict.
Our thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has made Tom-all-Alone's — and its singular, suffering inhabitant — impossible to look away from.
We'll be back next week, going deeper into Bleak House — a novel that always has more to yield.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens' great sprawling masterpiece apart — carefully — and marvel at what's inside.
Today's segment is called Law, Laughter, and Loose Threads — and if that sounds like it might describe the English legal system itself, that is entirely intentional.
We're looking at how Dickens constructs his assault on Chancery — the comedy, the fury, the strange poetry of it — and at the hidden threads that stitch his sprawling cast together.
With me today: Dr. Eleanor Hartley, novelist and creative-writing teacher, who reads every sentence Dickens writes as a craftsman reading a blueprint.
Professor James Blackstone, legal historian, who can tell us exactly what Chancery was — and exactly why we should still be angry about it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and five-time reader of Bleak House, who brings the irreplaceable perspective of someone who has lived with this novel across a lifetime.
Let's start in Chapter One — because Dickens doesn't waste a paragraph.

He gives us this extraordinary passage about the corrupting reach of Jarndyce and Jarndyce — not just on the litigants, but on every clerk, every solicitor, every boy who ever stood at a door and said his master was engaged.
Eleanor, let's start with you — what is Dickens actually doing, architecturally, in that passage?
What strikes me first is the sheer vertical range of the list he constructs — from the master with his impaling files all the way down to the copying-clerk.
Dickens is mapping an entire institution through its hierarchy of complicity — and the genius is that nobody is innocent, but nobody is purely villainous either.
And then there's that extraordinary list of nouns — listen to this opening:
"In trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation, botheration, under false pretences of all sorts, there are influences that can never come to good."
That accumulation — trickery, evasion, procrastination, spoliation — it's not just a list, it's a drumroll of moral degradation.
Each word is slightly worse than the last, and "botheration" — which sounds almost comic — lands like a slap, because it trivialises the whole catastrophe.
That tonal whiplash — the comic word in a tragic list — is absolutely characteristic of how Dickens keeps us off-balance.
Eleanor is quite right about the structure, and I'd add that the legal specificity is doing enormous work here.

The Six Clerks' Office was a real institution — abolished just twenty years before Bleak House was written — and Dickens' original readers would have known exactly what it was and exactly how it worked.
Chizzle, Mizzle, Drizzle — the absurd names sound like parody, but they stand in for a very real class of solicitors who made comfortable livings simply by keeping cases alive.
Chancery operated on fees, not outcomes — so delay was, structurally, the most profitable strategy available to everyone with a hand in the machinery.
Which is why Dickens says, later in the novel, with almost casual ferocity:
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
Seven words — and they are simply not wrong.
Dickens understood that the system's incoherence wasn't accidental — it was, from the right angle, perfectly coherent.
What I keep coming back to is that line at the very end of the passage — because it shifts register completely.
He's moved from specific clerks and solicitors to something much larger — a kind of moral atmosphere that settles over everyone, even observers.
Here — let me read it properly, because the rhythm matters enormously:
"Even those who have contemplated its history from the outermost circle of such evil have been insensibly tempted into a loose way of letting bad things alone to take their own bad course."
"Insensibly tempted" — that's the devastating phrase.
Not corrupted by violence or greed, but quietly, without noticing — the way you stop caring about a problem because it's always been there.
That indicts the reader, too, which I find almost unbearably precise.
Caroline has just put her finger on something I think is crucial to how the whole novel works as a system.
Dickens is constructing a world where passivity is a form of participation — where looking away is a moral act with consequences.
And that's why the famous rhetorical question in Chapter Sixteen lands with such extraordinary force.

"What connexion can there be between the place in Lincolnshire, the house in town, the Mercury in powder, and the whereabout of Jo the outlaw with the broom, who had that distant ray of light upon him when he swept the churchyard-step?"
Structurally, that question is doing two things at once — it's a genuine mystery, but it's also an argument.
Dickens is saying: these worlds are connected, whether you admit the connexion or not.
The "loose way of letting bad things alone" — that's what separates Lady Dedlock's world from Jo's, and Dickens is insisting it is not a natural separation.
The Mercury in powder is a lovely detail to fix on, because it represents an entire class of people whose profession is elaborate ornamental irrelevance.
The powdered footman is the Dedlock world's equivalent of the Chancery copying-clerk — doing meaningless work in service of a system that is self-perpetuating and morally hollow.
And Jo — who is designated explicitly as an outlaw, remember — Jo has no system.
He is outside every institution that might theoretically protect him, including the law that Dickens has just spent thirty-nine chapters destroying.
That phrase — "that distant ray of light upon him" — is not incidental.
In the Victorian visual tradition, a ray of light falling on a figure is divine grace, divine notice.
Dickens is quietly suggesting that God, at least, has noticed Jo — even if the law, the Church, and the gentry collectively have not.
I want to turn to the scene in Westminster Hall, near the end — because it's the moment where all of this fury becomes almost unbearably funny.
Esther and Allan arrive at the court and find it packed — something extraordinary is happening inside.
And Dickens describes it like this — through Esther's careful, slightly baffled narration:
"It appeared to be something droll, for occasionally there was a laugh and a cry of 'Silence!' It appeared to be something interesting, for every one was pushing and striving to get nearer."
And then — the lawyers.

"There were several young counsellors in wigs and whiskers on the outside of the crowd, and when one of them told the others about it, they put their hands in their pockets, and quite doubled themselves up with laughter, and went stamping about the pavement of the Hall."
The thing that destroys me is the wigs and whiskers — that specific, absurd detail.
These men are laughing at the collapse of a case that has consumed lives — and they look ridiculous doing it.
Dickens makes the comedy do the work of the indictment.
That triple anaphora — "It appeared to be something droll... it appeared to be something interesting" — that's Dickens at his most controlled.
The repetition creates suspense through indirection — Esther cannot see, so we cannot see, and the withheld information becomes almost unbearable.
And crucially, we are receiving this through Esther — the narrator who is constitutionally honest, who reports what she sees and does not embellish.
So the lawyers' hilarity, filtered through her steady gaze, becomes monstrous precisely because she doesn't say it is.
The dual narration — Esther and the omniscient voice — is Dickens' most audacious structural choice in the entire novel.
Each narrative mode has things the other cannot say — and Dickens calibrates exactly which voice to deploy and when.
The lawyers' laughter is, historically, entirely plausible — which is the most chilling thing about it.
Jarndyce and Jarndyce was modelled, quite closely, on real cases — Jennens versus Jennens most famously, which ran for decades and ended with the entire estate consumed in costs.
When such a case finally collapsed, the legal profession did, indeed, find it entertaining.
There's a contempt embedded in that laughter — for the suitors, for the idea that the court existed to serve anyone but itself.
Which returns us, perfectly, to Dickens' one great principle: the law exists to make business for itself.
And at the end of Jarndyce and Jarndyce, the business is complete — not because justice was served, but because there is nothing left to bill for.
And there it is — Dickens' great system, seen from every angle: polemical, structural, comic, and quietly devastating.
The law makes business for itself, the observers are insensibly corrupted, the lawyers stamp and double with laughter — and somewhere outside, Jo sweeps the step with a distant ray of light upon him.
Thank you to Eleanor, James, and Caroline for a conversation that has given me a great deal to sit with.
We'll be back with our next segment very soon.

segments.title: The Circumlocution Office and Its Victims: Where Stories Converge

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, where we move through Dickens's great novel chapter by chapter, passage by passage, trying to understand why it still feels so urgent.
Today we're looking at the machinery of power — the institutions that grind people down and the astonishing way Dickens renders them on the page.
With me, as always, are three guides I trust absolutely.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — she sees every gear.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal historian who knows what Chancery actually was, and what it cost the people trapped inside it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel — she's read it five times and still finds new things to love and to mourn.
Let's begin with Lady Dedlock — apparently untouchable, apparently inscrutable — and with Dickens's wickedly funny account of exactly how wrong she is about herself.
What I love about this passage is how gleefully Dickens demolishes Lady Dedlock's self-image before she even has a chance to defend it.
She believes herself to be, as Dickens puts it, an inscrutable Being — capital B — quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals.
"She supposes herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of ordinary mortals — seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks so."
That tiny parenthetical — where indeed she looks so — is devastating.
He grants her the mirror. He just refuses to grant her the reality it reflects.
And then the list of people who know her perfectly — from her maid to the manager of the Italian Opera — each one feeding her vanity while quietly steering her.
The tradespeople, the jewellers, the librarian Mr. Sladdery — they all understand her moral nature as precisely as her dressmaker understands her measurements.
And what Dickens does structurally there is remarkable — he builds that list into a kind of controlled crescendo.
Each item in the catalogue — a new dress, a new singer, a new dwarf or giant — is equal in weight, which is part of the comedy.
A new chapel sits right next to a new form of jewellery, and neither is treated as more significant than the other.
That levelling is Dickens's satire at its most precise — fashionable religion and fashionable accessories are one and the same currency.
But then comes the Gulliver simile, which just stops you cold.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The joke is that the simile flatters no one — Gulliver is ridiculous, Lilliput is ridiculous, and the whole aristocratic fleet is ridiculous for allowing itself to be towed.
What strikes me here, beyond the comedy, is how accurately it maps onto something real about class and commerce in the 1850s.
The relationship between the aristocracy and the luxury trades was genuinely symbiotic — and genuinely predatory in both directions.
Blaze and Sparkle, Sheen and Gloss — Dickens has named these tradespeople to make them sound like pantomime characters, which is precisely what they are to Lady Dedlock.
But the joke turns when you realize they understand the game and she does not.
Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, says without vanity that he can turn them round my finger — and Dickens tells us Sladdery does not exaggerate at all.
An honest man, managing dishonest people — who have convinced themselves they are above being managed.
And now contrast that with Vholes's office — because if the Lady Dedlock passage is comedy of the drawing room, the Vholes passage is comedy of the charnel house.
Dickens opens by saying the office is in disposition retiring and in situation retired — already it's retreating from view, from light, from any claim to being part of the civilized world.
It is squeezed up in a corner and blinks at a dead wall.
"Three feet of knotty-floored dark passage bring the client to Mr. Vholes's jet-black door, in an angle profoundly dark on the brightest midsummer morning."
Brightest midsummer morning — and still dark. The place is impervious to light itself.
And then there is the smell.

"A smell as of unwholesome sheep blending with the smell of must and dust is referable to the nightly — and often daily — consumption of mutton fat in candles and to the fretting of parchment forms and skins in greasy drawers."
Unwholesome sheep. Greasy drawers. The law rendered as carcass.
What Dickens does with that description is architecturally brilliant — every detail is both literal and emblematic at exactly the same moment.
The windows have a determination to be always dirty and always shut — that's not description, that's characterization.
He grants the windows a will — a stubborn, closed, opaque will — and in doing so describes Vholes himself without naming him once in the paragraph.
The office is a portrait. Vholes is its perfect inhabitant.
And then comes the passage where Dickens goes further — where he stops describing and starts accusing.

"Mr. Vholes, with his three daughters and his father in the Vale of Taunton, is continually doing duty, like a piece of timber, to shore up some decayed foundation that has become a pitfall and a nuisance."
A piece of timber. Not even a villain — just structural material for a corrupt edifice.
That timber metaphor is historically precise, whether Dickens intended it so or not.
The argument against Chancery reform, through the 1840s and into the 1850s, was almost never that Chancery was good.
It was that reform would harm the livelihoods of the people dependent on the system — the solicitors, the clerks, the copyists, the Vholeses.
Dickens captures the logic exactly — the question is never one of a change from wrong to right, which is quite an extraneous consideration.
"The question is never one of a change from wrong to right — which is quite an extraneous consideration — but is always one of injury or advantage to that eminently respectable legion, Vholes."
Eminently respectable legion. That phrase still makes me want to laugh and then feel bad about laughing.

There's a passage from Esther's narration that I think belongs in the same breath as all of this — because she experiences Chancery from the inside, and she is baffled by it in a way that's more devastating than satire.
She sits in the court and tries to reconcile the smooth ceremony with what she knows it is doing to people's lives.
The sickness of hope deferred — that phrase comes from Proverbs, and Dickens knows his readers will hear it.
And then Esther watches the Lord Chancellor and the whole court look at each other as if nothing is wrong at all.

"To behold the Lord Chancellor and the whole array of practitioners under him looking at one another and at the spectators as if nobody had ever heard that all over England the name in which they were assembled was a bitter jest —"
"— was held in universal horror, contempt, and indignation, was known for something so flagrant and bad that little short of a miracle could bring any good out of it to any one."
Little short of a miracle. And the court just carries on, in good order and composure.
And then Esther says she looked around and found only one thing real — poor little Miss Flite, the madwoman, standing on a bench and nodding at it.
That ending is one of the great strokes in the whole novel.
Esther — rational, observant, grounded Esther — loses her grip on what is real inside Chancery.
And the only anchor she finds is the woman the court has classified as mad.
Dickens is turning the sanity calculus completely inside out — Miss Flite is nodding because she understands what she's looking at.
The court, which maintains perfect composure, is the delusion. Miss Flite's nodding is the only honest response in the room.
And what makes that historically verifiable is that people like Miss Flite existed — there were real suitors who had spent decades in Chancery and lost everything, including their hold on reason.
The court records are full of them — ancient suits, properties long since wasted in legal costs, families destroyed across generations.
Dickens drew on a particular case — Jennens v. Jennens — which had been running since 1798 and was still unresolved when he was writing.
The fiction is exaggerated, but only slightly. The institutional reality was nearly as absurd — and far less entertaining.
What connects all of these passages, I think, is that Dickens shows us the same lie in different costumes.
Lady Dedlock believes a fiction about herself; Chancery maintains a fiction about its purpose; Vholes is propped up by a fiction about reform.
And in every case, the people with the least power are the ones who pay for it.
Next time we turn to character — to the people Dickens places inside these systems — and what happens to them when the machinery takes hold.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

segments.title: Redemption, Ruin, and the Cost of Truth

utterances.text: We've arrived at the closing movement of Bleak House — and it is, by any measure, a sombre one.
The novel's great machinery of plot has done its grinding work, and what remains is the human cost.
Jo is dying. Lady Dedlock is destroyed. Richard is fading. And Chesney Wold has gone very, very quiet.
I want to begin with Jo — with Eleanor, if I may — because Dickens builds toward that death with an image that has haunted readers for a hundred and seventy years.
Yes, and the image itself is almost shockingly simple — which is precisely why it works.
Dickens doesn't reach for grandeur when Jo is dying. He reaches for a cart.
A broken-down, utterly ordinary cart, dragging across stony ground.
He writes — and I think everyone should hear this at full weight —
"For the cart so hard to draw is near its journey's end and drags over stony ground."
That word "draw" is doing extraordinary work — drawing a cart, but also drawing out a life, and drawing a reader forward against their will.
And the clock image that follows — the broken steps, the worn mechanism — all of it says: this body has been used up by a world that never acknowledged it owned one.
What strikes me — and Eleanor's reading makes this sharper — is how precisely that image reflects Jo's actual legal and social position.
Jo is not, in the eyes of Victorian law, a person who can be wronged in any actionable sense.
He can be moved on, he can be used as a witness, he can die — and the machinery of the state simply continues.
The cart is not a sentimental figure. It is a precise one. Jo has been in harness from the moment we met him.
Dickens understood — with a ferocity the novel never quite loses — that poverty isn't misfortune. It is a system.
I can't read that passage without feeling the thing physically — that weight, that exhaustion.
When I first read it as a teenager I didn't understand what Dickens was doing structurally. I just knew I felt crushed.
And I think that's the point — the affect arrives before the argument. You feel the injustice before you've named it.
That line — "Not many times can the sun rise and behold it still upon its weary road" — has a kind of biblical cadence that makes it almost unbearable.
The sun is a witness. And still no one saves him.
The sun as witness — which brings us to another kind of exposure entirely.
Because while Jo's story ends in quiet erasure, Lady Dedlock's ends in something almost operatically public.
James — the collapse of her world happens in a single paragraph that feels like a building falling down.
It does — and the sentence structure performs the collapse in real time. Listen to what Dickens actually does.
He begins with two words that serve as a verdict:
"So! All is broken down."
That exclamation mark after "So" is one of the most devastating punctuation marks in Victorian fiction.
It is not surprise. It is completion. The thing that was always going to happen has happened.
And then the sentence piles charge upon charge — name, husband, shame, murder — each one a separate indignity, each one worse than the last.
The law she built her life around — the law of reputation, of appearances — has turned on her with perfect symmetry.
That phrase "may be spreading while she thinks about it" is the moment I always stop and re-read.
Because the shame isn't just public — it is happening faster than consciousness can track it.
It's almost a premonition of how information moves now — viral, unstoppable, indifferent to the person at the centre.
And structurally, Dickens has been preparing this moment since the very first chapter — the fog, the Court, the secret buried in the mud of London.
When it breaks, it breaks with the full force of everything that was ever compressed into silence.
There's something I find almost unbearable about her being accused of murder on top of everything else.
She's already been destroyed by exposure. And then Dickens adds one more charge — false, of course — as if the world needed another reason to condemn her.
It speaks to something Dickens understood about how scandal works — once a reputation cracks, anything becomes believable.
And the novel doesn't grant her a public vindication — only silence and marble.
Eleanor, you've written about the Chesney Wold passages in the final chapters — the hush that settles over everything.
The Chesney Wold ending is one of the most controlled pieces of Gothic satire Dickens ever wrote.
He gives us an image of institutional suppression — Sir Leicester buying silence — but then immediately undercuts it.
The rumour doesn't die. It just becomes lame. Listen to how he phrases it:
"It is a lame story, feebly whispering and creeping about, and any brighter spark of life it shows soon dies away."
The story about the story is itself described as a dying thing. It's recursive — and it's brilliant.
The suppression of truth, in Dickens, never quite works. It leaves a residue — a whisper, a creep, a lame and persistent ghost.
That image of the old aristocratic women with their large fans — "like charmers reduced to flirting with grim death" — is one of Dickens' most savage satirical strokes.
These are the women who enforced Lady Dedlock's social world, who policed its codes, who now gossip about her desecrating the family mausoleum.
And Dickens' response to their judgment — the dead Dedlocks taking it all "very calmly" — is quiet devastation.
The dead are indifferent to class. It is only the living who maintain these fictions — and they look absurd doing it.
What moves me in this ending — really moves me — is Esther watching Richard disappear.
Because he doesn't vanish all at once. He vanishes in glimpses.
Esther writes — and I always find this sentence stops me cold:
"His old light-hearted manner was all gone, but it shone out of him sometimes as I had occasionally known little momentary glimpses of my own old face to look out upon me from the glass."
She's describing his dissolution — but the image she reaches for is her own face in a mirror.
They are twins in damage. Chancery has done to him what smallpox did to her — erased the surface, left something altered and diminished underneath.
And then — "His laugh had not quite left him either, but it was like the echo of a joyful sound, and that is always sorrowful."
That's one of the great sentences in the novel. It says so much about how loss works — not total, not clean, just endlessly echoing.
The dual narration does something extraordinary here that I don't think gets discussed enough.
The omniscient narrator gives us Jo's death and Lady Dedlock's ruin in prose of controlled, almost liturgical gravity.
But Esther gives us Richard's decay in the language of intimacy — comparison, qualification, the small noticed detail.
Two registers of tragedy. One public, one private. And Dickens holds them in tension to the very end.
Two registers of tragedy — that feels like the right place to leave it.
Bleak House ends not with resolution but with residue — the lame story still creeping, the laugh still echoing, the cart finally still.
My deepest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done genuine justice to an extraordinary novel.
Bleak House Unpacked will return. Until then — keep reading.

c1:p1.text:
Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and
meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers
of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.
Fog on the Essex marshes, fog on the Kentish heights. Fog creeping
into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards and
hovering in the rigging of great ships; fog drooping on the gunwales
of barges and small boats. Fog in the eyes and throats of ancient
Greenwich pensioners, wheezing by the firesides of their wards; fog
in the stem and bowl of the afternoon pipe of the wrathful skipper,
down in his close cabin; fog cruelly pinching the toes and fingers of
his shivering little ’prentice boy on deck. Chance people on the
bridges peeping over the parapets into a nether sky of fog, with fog
all round them, as if they were up in a balloon and hanging in the
misty clouds.
c1:p1.summary: Fog blankets London from the Thames to the marshes, penetrating every space and afflicting everyone from Greenwich pensioners to cabin boys, creating an all-encompassing sense of obscurity and misery.
c1:p1.best_quote: Fog everywhere. Fog up the river, where it flows among green aits and meadows; fog down the river, where it rolls defiled among the tiers of shipping and the waterside pollutions of a great (and dirty) city.

c1:p3.text:
The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the
muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction,
appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old
corporation, Temple Bar. And hard by Temple Bar, in Lincoln’s Inn
Hall, at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor in
his High Court of Chancery.
c1:p3.summary: The fog and mud are thickest at Temple Bar and Lincoln's Inn Hall, where the Lord High Chancellor sits in the High Court of Chancery at the heart of murk.
c1:p3.best_quote: The raw afternoon is rawest, and the dense fog is densest, and the muddy streets are muddiest near that leaden-headed old obstruction, appropriate ornament for the threshold of a leaden-headed old corporation, Temple Bar.

c1:p5.text:
On such an afternoon, if ever, the Lord High Chancellor ought to be
sitting here—as here he is—with a foggy glory round his head,
softly fenced in with crimson cloth and curtains, addressed by a
large advocate with great whiskers, a little voice, and an
interminable brief, and outwardly directing his contemplation to the
lantern in the roof, where he can see nothing but fog. On such an
afternoon some score of members of the High Court of Chancery bar
ought to be—as here they are—mistily engaged in one of the ten
thousand stages of an endless cause, tripping one another up on
slippery precedents, groping knee-deep in technicalities, running
their goat-hair and horsehair warded heads against walls of words and
making a pretence of equity with serious faces, as players might. On
such an afternoon the various solicitors in the cause, some two or
three of whom have inherited it from their fathers, who made a
fortune by it, ought to be—as are they not?—ranged in a line, in a
long matted well (but you might look in vain for truth at the bottom
of it) between the registrar’s red table and the silk gowns, with
bills, cross-bills, answers, rejoinders, injunctions, affidavits,
issues, references to masters, masters’ reports, mountains of costly
nonsense, piled before them. Well may the court be dim, with wasting
candles here and there; well may the fog hang heavy in it, as if it
would never get out; well may the stained-glass windows lose their
colour and admit no light of day into the place; well may the
uninitiated from the streets, who peep in through the glass panes in
the door, be deterred from entrance by its owlish aspect and by the
drawl, languidly echoing to the roof from the padded dais where the
Lord High Chancellor looks into the lantern that has no light in it
and where the attendant wigs are all stuck in a fog-bank! This is the
Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted
lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every
madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined
suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and
begging through the round of every man’s acquaintance, which gives to
monied might the means abundantly of wearying out the right, which so
exhausts finances, patience, courage, hope, so overthrows the brain
and breaks the heart, that there is not an honourable man among its
practitioners who would not give—who does not often give—the
warning, “Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come
here!”
c1:p5.summary: An extended satirical tableau of the Lord Chancellor and court staff in their fog-wrapped surroundings, processing endless technicalities while suitors are ruined financially and psychologically; Chancery has destroyed lives across the nation.
c1:p5.best_quote: This is the Court of Chancery, which has its decaying houses and its blighted lands in every shire, which has its worn-out lunatic in every madhouse and its dead in every churchyard, which has its ruined suitor with his slipshod heels and threadbare dress borrowing and begging through the round of every man's acquaintance.

c29:p0.text:
Chesney Wold is shut up, carpets are rolled into great scrolls in
corners of comfortless rooms, bright damask does penance in brown
holland, carving and gilding puts on mortification, and the Dedlock
ancestors retire from the light of day again. Around and around the
house the leaves fall thick, but never fast, for they come circling
down with a dead lightness that is sombre and slow. Let the gardener
sweep and sweep the turf as he will, and press the leaves into full
barrows, and wheel them off, still they lie ankle-deep. Howls the
shrill wind round Chesney Wold; the sharp rain beats, the windows
rattle, and the chimneys growl. Mists hide in the avenues, veil the
points of view, and move in funeral-wise across the rising grounds.
On all the house there is a cold, blank smell like the smell of a
little church, though something dryer, suggesting that the dead and
buried Dedlocks walk there in the long nights and leave the flavour
of their graves behind them.
c29:p0.summary: Chesney Wold is shuttered and decaying as autumn arrives, described through vivid Gothic imagery of mist, wind, and the ghostly presence of deceased family members.
c29:p0.best_quote: the dead and buried Dedlocks walk there in the long nights and leave the flavour of their graves behind them

c17:p0.text:
Richard very often came to see us while we remained in London (though
he soon failed in his letter-writing), and with his quick abilities,
his good spirits, his good temper, his gaiety and freshness, was
always delightful. But though I liked him more and more the better I
knew him, I still felt more and more how much it was to be regretted
that he had been educated in no habits of application and
concentration. The system which had addressed him in exactly the same
manner as it had addressed hundreds of other boys, all varying in
character and capacity, had enabled him to dash through his tasks,
always with fair credit and often with distinction, but in a fitful,
dazzling way that had confirmed his reliance on those very qualities
in himself which it had been most desirable to direct and train. They
were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously
won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were
very bad masters. If they had been under Richard’s direction, they
would have been his friends; but Richard being under their direction,
they became his enemies.
c17:p0.summary: Esther reflects on Richard's natural talents being undermined by his lack of discipline, a problem rooted in an educational system that addresses all students identically rather than according to individual capacity.
c17:p0.best_quote: They were good qualities, without which no high place can be meritoriously won, but like fire and water, though excellent servants, they were very bad masters.

c39:p43.text:
Richard, emerging from the heavy shade of Symond’s Inn into the
sunshine of Chancery Lane—for there happens to be sunshine there
to-day—walks thoughtfully on, and turns into Lincoln’s Inn, and
passes under the shadow of the Lincoln’s Inn trees. On many such
loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on
the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering
step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and
consumed, the life turned sour. This lounger is not shabby yet, but
that may come. Chancery, which knows no wisdom but in precedent, is
very rich in such precedents; and why should one be different from
ten thousand?
c39:p43.summary: Richard emerges into sunshine and walks through Lincoln's Inn, but the narrator reflects on how the space has witnessed the deterioration of many Chancery suitors before him, suggesting he may follow the same path.
c39:p43.best_quote: On many such loungers have the speckled shadows of those trees often fallen; on the like bent head, the bitten nail, the lowering eye, the lingering step, the purposeless and dreamy air, the good consuming and consumed, the life turned sour.

c39:p44.text:
Yet the time is so short since his depreciation began that as he
saunters away, reluctant to leave the spot for some long months
together, though he hates it, Richard himself may feel his own case
as if it were a startling one. While his heart is heavy with
corroding care, suspense, distrust, and doubt, it may have room for
some sorrowful wonder when he recalls how different his first visit
there, how different he, how different all the colours of his mind.
But injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being
defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat;
from the impalpable suit which no man alive can understand, the time
for that being long gone by, it has become a gloomy relief to turn to
the palpable figure of the friend who would have saved him from this
ruin and make HIM his enemy. Richard has told Vholes the truth. Is he
in a hardened or a softened mood, he still lays his injuries equally
at that door; he was thwarted, in that quarter, of a set purpose, and
that purpose could only originate in the one subject that is
resolving his existence into itself; besides, it is a justification
to him in his own eyes to have an embodied antagonist and oppressor.
c39:p44.summary: The narrator analyzes how Richard's corruption has progressed: unable to combat the abstract suit, he has seized upon Jarndyce as a concrete enemy and embodiment of all his injuries, justifying himself with the logic of having an enemy.
c39:p44.best_quote: injustice breeds injustice; the fighting with shadows and being defeated by them necessitates the setting up of substances to combat

c51:p27.text:
“Nor I,” said Richard moodily. “Who ever did?” He brightened again in
a moment and said with his natural openness, “Woodcourt, I should be
sorry to be misunderstood by you, even if I gained by it in your
estimation. You must know that I have done no good this long time. I
have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of
nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out
of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not,
though I dare say you will soon hear, if you have not already heard,
a very different opinion. To make short of a long story, I am afraid
I have wanted an object; but I have an object now—or it has me—and
it is too late to discuss it. Take me as I am, and make the best of
me.”
c51:p27.summary: Richard confesses to Woodcourt that he has accomplished nothing, lacks purpose, and feels trapped by fate and the Chancery suit, yet demands acceptance without judgment.
c51:p27.best_quote: I have not intended to do much harm, but I seem to have been capable of nothing else. It may be that I should have done better by keeping out of the net into which my destiny has worked me, but I think not.

c60:p96.text:
We sat down to dinner, and I had an opportunity of observing Richard,
anxiously. I was not disturbed by Mr. Vholes (who took off his gloves
to dine), though he sat opposite to me at the small table, for I
doubt if, looking up at all, he once removed his eyes from his host’s
face. I found Richard thin and languid, slovenly in his dress,
abstracted in his manner, forcing his spirits now and then, and at
other intervals relapsing into a dull thoughtfulness. About his large
bright eyes that used to be so merry there was a wanness and a
restlessness that changed them altogether. I cannot use the
expression that he looked old. There is a ruin of youth which is not
like age, and into such a ruin Richard’s youth and youthful beauty
had all fallen away.
c60:p96.summary: Esther observes Richard's alarming physical decline: he is thin, languid, slovenly, abstracted, with dull eyes instead of his old merry brightness, embodying a tragic ruin of youth.
c60:p96.best_quote: There is a ruin of youth which is not like age, and into such a ruin Richard's youth and youthful beauty had all fallen away.

c51:p59.text:
His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his
despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in
its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so
conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched
me to the heart. But the commentary upon it now indelibly written in
his handsome face made it far more distressing than it used to be. I
say indelibly, for I felt persuaded that if the fatal cause could
have been for ever terminated, according to his brightest visions, in
that same hour, the traces of the premature anxiety, self-reproach,
and disappointment it had occasioned him would have remained upon his
features to the hour of his death.
c51:p59.summary: Esther reflects deeply on the tragedy of Richard's forced optimism, which has worn itself into his face as permanent marks of anxiety and self-reproach that will outlast any resolution of the suit.
c51:p59.best_quote: His hopefulness had long been more painful to me than his despondency; it was so unlike hopefulness, had something so fierce in its determination to be it, was so hungry and eager, and yet so conscious of being forced and unsustainable that it had long touched me to the heart.

c2:p2.text:
My Lady Dedlock has returned to her house in town for a few days
previous to her departure for Paris, where her ladyship intends to
stay some weeks, after which her movements are uncertain. The
fashionable intelligence says so for the comfort of the Parisians,
and it knows all fashionable things. To know things otherwise were to
be unfashionable. My Lady Dedlock has been down at what she calls, in
familiar conversation, her “place” in Lincolnshire. The waters are
out in Lincolnshire. An arch of the bridge in the park has been
sapped and sopped away. The adjacent low-lying ground for half a mile
in breadth is a stagnant river with melancholy trees for islands in
it and a surface punctured all over, all day long, with falling rain.
My Lady Dedlock’s place has been extremely dreary. The weather for
many a day and night has been so wet that the trees seem wet through,
and the soft loppings and prunings of the woodman’s axe can make no
crash or crackle as they fall. The deer, looking soaked, leave
quagmires where they pass. The shot of a rifle loses its sharpness in
the moist air, and its smoke moves in a tardy little cloud towards
the green rise, coppice-topped, that makes a background for the
falling rain. The view from my Lady Dedlock’s own windows is
alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink. The vases
on the stone terrace in the foreground catch the rain all day; and
the heavy drops fall—drip, drip, drip—upon the broad flagged
pavement, called from old time the Ghost’s Walk, all night. On
Sundays the little church in the park is mouldy; the oaken pulpit
breaks out into a cold sweat; and there is a general smell and taste
as of the ancient Dedlocks in their graves. My Lady Dedlock (who is
childless), looking out in the early twilight from her boudoir at a
keeper’s lodge and seeing the light of a fire upon the latticed
panes, and smoke rising from the chimney, and a child, chased by a
woman, running out into the rain to meet the shining figure of a
wrapped-up man coming through the gate, has been put quite out of
temper. My Lady Dedlock says she has been “bored to death.”
c2:p2.summary: Lady Dedlock returns to her Lincolnshire estate before departing for Paris, where the landscape is depicted as relentlessly dreary and sodden; her observation of a family scene at a keeper's lodge disrupts her usual composure.
c2:p2.best_quote: The view from my Lady Dedlock's own windows is alternately a lead-coloured view and a view in Indian ink

c12:p116.text:
Mr. Tulkinghorn does so with deference and holds it open while she
passes out. She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner
and insolent grace. They meet again at dinner—again, next
day—again, for many days in succession. Lady Dedlock is always the
same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable
to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine. Mr.
Tulkinghorn is always the same speechless repository of noble
confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home. They
appear to take as little note of one another as any two people
enclosed within the same walls could. But whether each evermore
watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great
reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the
other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know
how much the other knows—all this is hidden, for the time, in their
own hearts.
